title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of FirstEnergy Service Company to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 09/23/2026 Answer re Interim Resource Adequacy Service filing under ER26-3515.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.           )       Docket No. ER26-3515-000


 MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER OF FIRSTENERGY
                       SERVICE COMPANY

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,

FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates (“FirstEnergy”), respectfully moves for

leave to answer and submits this limited answer to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s September 23,

2026 Answer (“PJM Answer”) to various comments and protests addressing PJM’s Interim

Resource Adequacy Service filing (“IRAS Filing”). Although Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits

answers to protests and answers to answers, the Commission accepts otherwise-prohibited answers

that clarify the record or assist its decision-making.1 Good cause exists here because PJM leaves

material arguments in FirstEnergy’s Limited Protest and Comments (“FirstEnergy Protest and

Comments”) unanswered and advances no compelling new law or facts that defeat FirstEnergy’s

remaining objections. As the filing entity, PJM bears the burden under section 205 of the Federal

Power Act.2 Its assertion that silence should not be treated as acceptance3 does not satisfy that




       1
        18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2025); see Baltimore Gas & Electric Co. v. Columbia
Gas Transmission, LLC, 193 FERC ¶ 61,036, at P 34 & n.28 (2025) (accepting answers to
answers because they provided information that assisted the Commission’s decision-making).
       2
        16 U.S.C. § 824d(a)-(b); Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028,
1035 (D.C. Cir. 2022); NorthWestern Corp. v. FERC, 884 F.3d 1176, 1182–83 (D.C. Cir. 2018);
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,050, at P 23 (2026).
       3
          PJM Answer at 8 n.23 (“While PJM’s answer does not address every argument raised
by intervenors, silence on any argument should not be deemed as acceptance of the arguments
raised.”).
 burden. The Commission, therefore, should grant the relief requested in the FirstEnergy Protest

and Comments.


I.     LIMITED ANSWER

       A.      PJM Fails to Respond to Issues Raised by FirstEnergy That Are Material to
               the Justness and Reasonableness of PJM’s IRAS Filing.
       PJM fails to address a number of issues raised by FirstEnergy in its Protest and Comments.

Most notably, PJM does not address FirstEnergy’s argument that its IRAS proposal improperly

denies certain new large loads and associated generation access to the Fixed Resource Requirement

(“FRR”) Alternative. As FirstEnergy explained, PJM’s proposal would permit new data-center

load and associated generation within an existing FRR Service Area to remain outside the

Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”), while requiring Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”)

resources associated with new loads outside an existing FRR Service Area to participate in RPM.

       FirstEnergy explained that Schedule 8.1, section B of the Reliability Assurance Agreement

(“RAA”) permits an eligible Load Serving Entity (“LSE”) to demonstrate that “all or part” of its

load falls within the RAA’s FRR Service Area definition and is supported by sufficient Capacity

Resources. FirstEnergy, accordingly, argued that the “all or part” language contemplates use of

the FRR Alternative for less than all of an eligible LSE’s load and that PJM has not justified

denying new load and associated generation outside an existing FRR Service Area a comparable

opportunity to use the FRR Alternative.4 PJM addresses other FRR issues but not FirstEnergy’s

argument. PJM, therefore, has not rebutted FirstEnergy’s showing or carried its section 205 burden

to justify the different treatment of new load and associated generation inside and outside existing

FRR Service Areas.


       4
        FirstEnergy Protest at 6-7 & n.19 (citing PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement,
Schedule 8.1, section B).


                                                     2
        PJM also does not squarely address several other FirstEnergy objections. PJM explains

generally why IRAS distinguishes between new and existing load, but does not explain how its

June 1, 2027 in-service date protects existing commercial arrangements or agreements nearing

completion when the IRAS Proposal was filed. PJM likewise explains why existing Capacity

Resources should not qualify as BYONC, but does not address FirstEnergy’s distinct argument

that an Energy Resource, which is not presently a Capacity Resource, should be eligible to qualify

as new capacity for purposes of BYONC. Nor does PJM substantively address FirstEnergy’s

objection to terminating IRAS after three consecutive years of sufficient capacity, even though

subsequent large-load additions could recreate the shortfall.        PJM likewise fails to rebut

FirstEnergy’s objection that the annual reallocation of IRAS curtailment obligations could unduly

favor a new large load by reducing its obligation solely because unrelated generation enters or

other load exits the region, even though the load itself has not brought capacity. PJM further offers

no response to FirstEnergy’s objection to crediting a load with Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”) capacity when that load was not included in the forecast supporting the procurement.5

       Finally, although PJM separately clarifies that the capacity and Registry-reporting

obligations fall on LSEs and that Electric Distributors receive load-reduction directives, it does

not address FirstEnergy’s broader request that the proposed provisions consistently identify the

entity responsible for each IRAS requirement. 6 Clear assignment of those responsibilities is

essential to effective planning, implementation, compliance, and enforcement.


       B.       Where PJM Does Respond to FirstEnergy, Its Arguments Are Unconvincing


       5
         FirstEnergy Protest at 7-9 (transition and existing commercial arrangements), 13-14
(Energy Resources), 14-15 (termination of IRAS), 15-16 (allocation of RBP capacity), 16-17
(reallocation of curtailment obligations).
       6
           FirstEnergy Protest at 12-13; see also PJM Answer at 13, 17-18, 26-30.


                                                     3
         First, PJM claims that requiring BYONC resources to participate in RPM for ten years

ensures that the capacity is “real and lasting.” 7 That rationale may support requiring an

enforceable, durable capacity commitment, but it does not demonstrate that mandatory RPM

participation for ten consecutive Delivery Years is reasonably tailored to that objective. PJM does

not adequately explain why continued capacity availability could not be secured through the

commercial arrangement supporting the resource or another enforceable commitment tied to the

associated load. PJM, therefore, has not established that the specific ten-year RPM participation

requirement is just and reasonable under section 205.

        Second, PJM’s response does not cure the jurisdictional defect identified by FirstEnergy.

PJM characterizes the payment as compensation to an LSE for a wholesale load-reduction service

and establishes a default rate equal to 50 percent of the Non-Performance Charge Rate. Yet PJM

permits state and retail regulatory authorities to reduce that purportedly wholesale rate, including

to zero, and to determine which entities receive the compensation and which retail customers fund

it.8 That substantial state control over the amount and allocation of the payment reinforces, rather

than resolves, FirstEnergy’s objection that the proposed mechanism concerns retail rates and

service. Nor does characterizing the LSE as the initial recipient change the fact that the PJM tariff

creates a compensation framework based on curtailment that will ultimately be implemented at the

retail level.    PJM’s reliance on FERC v. Electric Power Supply Association and Tri-State

Generation and Transmission Association, Inc. does not defeat that objection.9 As PJM describes



        7
            PJM Answer at 43 & n.161; see also FirstEnergy Protest at 5-6, 15.
        8
            PJM Answer at 54-58; see also FirstEnergy Protest at 3-5.
        9
         PJM Answer at 19-30, 54-58 (citing FERC v. Electric Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S.
260 (2016), and Tri-State Generation & Transmission Association, Inc., 196 FERC ¶ 61,127
(2026)).


                                                      4
 it, Tri-State emphasized that the jurisdictional utility’s members retained discretion whether to

flow the relevant terms through to their retail contracts. Here, by contrast, the PJM tariff itself

would establish a default compensation mechanism based on load reductions that will ultimately

be implemented at the retail level. PJM’s cited authorities therefore do not establish that the

challenged compensation mechanism falls within FERC’s jurisdiction.

       Third, PJM does not adequately justify applying the proposed Large Load definition to

manufacturing and other industrial facilities. Although PJM asserts that FirstEnergy identified no

basis for treating those facilities differently from data centers, it does not address FirstEnergy’s

explanation that, unlike data centers, short-notice curtailment of manufacturing facilities may

disrupt production and supply chains, strand inventory, damage equipment, and require costly

cleaning and restart procedures. Those differences bear directly on whether subjecting both

categories of load to the same IRAS obligations is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory.

PJM, therefore, should be required to address those differences and justify the proposed treatment

of manufacturing and other industrial facilities before subjecting them to the same IRAS

requirements as data centers.10

       Finally, PJM’s assertion that it does not presently perceive a connection between the Large

Load Registry and the forthcoming pro forma transmission-service agreement does not

demonstrate that finalizing the Registry now will avoid overlapping, inconsistent, or duplicative

requirements.11

       FirstEnergy does not dispute that large-load growth presents resource-adequacy concerns

requiring action. But the need for some action does not establish that each component of PJM’s



       10
            FirstEnergy Protest at 10–11; PJM Answer at 14–16.
       11
            PJM Answer at 14 n.47; see also FirstEnergy Protest at 11-12.


                                                     5
 proposal satisfies section 205. PJM leaves material FirstEnergy arguments unrebutted and, as to

the arguments it addresses, advances no compelling new law or facts that defeat FirstEnergy’s

specific objections.


II.    CONCLUSION
       For these reasons, FirstEnergy respectfully requests that the Commission accept this

limited Answer, grant the relief requested in the FirstEnergy Protest and Comments, and direct

PJM to correct the identified deficiencies through a compliance filing.
